characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: Technical Feasibility Strategy focuses on proving that Danish digital identity can operate without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google platforms. It drives the design, construction, and evaluation of non‑production demonstrators—such as FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS and browser‑based or hardware‑token fallback paths—that showcase secure, standards‑based access. Success is measured by completed demonstrators, a published risk report, and technical evidence that platform‑neutral authentication meets eIDAS and NSIS security thresholds. The strategy also informs procurement language and policy proposals, ensuring that technical viability underpins all subsequent advocacy and procurement actions.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: By delivering concrete demonstrators, Technical Feasibility Strategy provides the evidence base that Policy Advocacy Strategy can leverage to frame resilience arguments, and it equips Procurement Influence Strategy with hard data to justify platform‑neutral language in tender documents. The technical proof also strengthens Coalition Building Strategy’s credibility when rallying stakeholders.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: The focus on narrow, high‑security demonstrators can clash with EU Standards Engagement Strategy, which may prioritize broader interoperability requirements that differ from the chosen technologies. Additionally, an aggressive technical agenda may strain Coalition Building Strategy if stakeholders demand features beyond the demonstrator scope, creating friction over resource allocation.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: Policy Advocacy Strategy shapes the legislative and procurement environment to reduce Denmark’s digital identity dependence on foreign platforms. It frames the issue as a resilience and continuity risk, linking supplier concentration to strategic autonomy, and crafts policy proposals that embed platform‑neutral and fallback authentication requirements into AltID and related procurement documents. Success is measured by the number of formal policy submissions, the adoption of platform‑neutral language in official documents, and the measurable increase in stakeholder support for resilience‑focused procurement. The strategy also coordinates with coalition partners to amplify messaging and with procurement experts to translate policy into actionable tender clauses.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy gains strength from Coalition Building Strategy’s broad stakeholder base and from Technical Feasibility Strategy’s demonstrators, which provide empirical evidence to support policy arguments. Together, they create a compelling narrative that procurement bodies can adopt, while also informing EU Standards Engagement Strategy with concrete policy requirements.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy may conflict with Technical Feasibility Strategy if policy pushes for features that exceed current technical demonstrator capabilities, creating a gap between policy ambition and proof. It can also clash with EU Standards Engagement Strategy when national policy priorities diverge from EU interoperability norms, risking misalignment in cross‑border identity frameworks.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: Coalition Building Strategy assembles a diverse network of civil‑society groups, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, and internal stakeholders from the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen. Its goal is to create a unified front that amplifies resilience and platform‑neutral messaging, ensuring that advocacy efforts resonate across political, technical, and commercial arenas. Success is measured by the breadth and depth of stakeholder engagement, the number of joint statements issued, and the tangible influence on policy and procurement discussions. The strategy also manages internal alignment to prevent conflicting priorities from diluting the coalition’s impact.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Coalition Building Strategy strengthens Policy Advocacy Strategy by providing a broad base of supporters, and it reinforces Procurement Influence Strategy by creating political pressure that procurement bodies must heed. The coalition also supplies a platform for Technical Feasibility Strategy to showcase demonstrators to a wider audience, enhancing credibility.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition Building Strategy can clash with Technical Feasibility Strategy if coalition demands features beyond the demonstrator scope, forcing a shift in technical priorities. It may also conflict with EU Standards Engagement Strategy when coalition members push for national standards that diverge from EU interoperability goals, creating tension between domestic advocacy and European alignment.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: Procurement Influence Strategy targets the AltID procurement process and related tender documents to embed platform‑neutral and fallback authentication requirements. It translates technical evidence and policy arguments into concrete procurement clauses, scoring criteria, and vendor evaluation rubrics that reward reduced reliance on Apple and Google. Success is measured by the inclusion of platform‑neutral language in official procurement documents, the number of vendors meeting the new criteria, and the measurable reduction in platform concentration risk. The strategy also monitors procurement outcomes to ensure that the mandated requirements are enforced and that vendors cannot game the system through technical workarounds.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Procurement Influence Strategy relies on Technical Feasibility Strategy’s demonstrators to justify platform‑neutral clauses, and it is amplified by Policy Advocacy Strategy’s framing of resilience risk. The coalition’s political pressure further strengthens procurement arguments, while EU Standards Engagement Strategy can help align procurement language with emerging European interoperability norms.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement Influence Strategy may conflict with EU Standards Engagement Strategy if procurement clauses diverge from EU interoperability requirements, risking misalignment. It can also clash with Coalition Building Strategy when political pressure forces procurement to adopt overly prescriptive language that limits vendor flexibility, potentially alienating coalition partners who favor broader technical solutions.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: EU Standards Engagement Strategy positions Denmark as a proactive contributor to the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, advocating for platform‑neutral and fallback authentication mechanisms that align with eIDAS2 and NSIS. It monitors EU working groups, submits technical and policy input, and champions a sovereign‑identity sandbox to test new models. Success is measured by the adoption of platform‑neutral language in EU standards documents, the inclusion of fallback authentication requirements in the Digital Identity Wallet specification, and the extent to which Danish policy and procurement language are reflected in European interoperability guidelines.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy benefits from Technical Feasibility Strategy’s demonstrators, which provide concrete evidence for standard proposals, and from Procurement Influence Strategy’s language that can be mirrored in EU specifications. It also leverages Coalition Building Strategy to rally domestic support for EU‑level advocacy.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy may clash with Policy Advocacy Strategy when national policy priorities conflict with EU interoperability norms, risking a fragmented stance. It can also conflict with Coalition Building Strategy if coalition members push for national standards that diverge from EU guidance, creating tension between domestic advocacy and European alignment.
